name: inko
desc: Safe and concurrent object-oriented programming language
why: A young concurrent object-oriented language with its own ownership model, unusual enough to be worth a look.

brief.what_it_is: Inko is a statically typed, object-oriented programming language for concurrent software. Source code goes in as .inko files, which are compiled to native machine code through LLVM and statically linked against a small runtime library written in Rust. The runtime handles process scheduling and non-blocking IO. The language is built around single ownership with move semantics, borrowing through ref and mut, lightweight processes that communicate by messages, and Result-based error handling with try and throw. The homepage and README do not name a version or describe a command-line interface beyond the inko executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Inko exists to make concurrent software easy to build 'without having to worry about unpredictable performance, unexpected runtime errors, data races, and type errors.' The README adds that it aims to be 'a compelling alternative to the likes of Ruby, Erlang, and Go', and not to compete with C and Rust.
brief.how_it_works: Memory is managed deterministically: values start out owned and are dropped when they go out of scope, with no garbage collector. Values can be borrowed immutably with ref or mutably with mut, and moved, and the compiler checks these uses. Concurrency uses lightweight processes defined as async types, which are isolated and communicate by sending messages. The compiler requires data sent between processes to be unique (uni), which removes the need for deep copying.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no install steps. It points to the 'Installing Inko' guide in the Inko manual at https://docs.inko-lang.org/manual/main/setup/installation/. The compiler uses LLVM as its backend, so an LLVM toolchain is probably needed, but I did not confirm the exact requirements from the guide, and I did not read that page.
brief.standout: Single ownership with move semantics and borrowing, applied without a garbage collector, is the unusual part. The concurrency model is described as inspired by Erlang and Pony, with compile-time checks that message data is unique, so the data is moved between processes and not copied.
brief.status: unknown. Neither the homepage nor the GitHub README shows a release version, release date, or last-commit date. The project has an active-looking site, a Discord server, and a GitHub repository, and nothing in the pages suggests it has been abandoned. The scout note calls it a young language.
brief.caveats: The README does not state a version, so the language may still change. Compilation depends on LLVM. The README says Inko does not aim to compete with low-level languages such as C and Rust on performance. Source is under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. Several homepage snippets are deliberately incorrect, such as one Stack example that includes a commented type error, so they are illustrations and not runnable as written. The install guide was not read.
quotes: A language for building concurrent software with confidence
Inko doesn't rely on garbage collection to manage memory. Instead, Inko relies on single ownership and move semantics.
Inko aims to be an efficient language, though it doesn't aim to compete with low-level languages such as C and Rust.
